rows.en: It is very, very astonishing to us about the masters of the Mishnah and the Talmud, who sought for themselves places enough to record various enactments that the heads of the early generations enacted, and did not find even a small place to record so great an enactment as this: to say when the Holy Writings were sealed and who sealed them. But in truth the matter is clear: the sealing of the Holy Writings was revealed and known to them, and the one who sealed the whole of all the books makes the act of sealing known explicitly in writing. Therefore they did not specify this enactment separately but only hinted at it in various places, because for them the existence of the sealing was an established assumption, which there is no need to spell out, so well known was it. But there are a great many hints in the words of the sages that point to the sealing. An excellent hint is given us in an aggadah told about the Scroll of Esther. It is told that Mordecai and Esther sent to the sages that the letter of Purim should be written for the generations. At first they refused, until the Holy One, blessed be He, enlightened their eyes, and they found it written in the Torah, in the Prophets and in the Writings. And they interpreted the words of the verse "and it was written in the book" (Esther 9:32) as referring to the Writings (Yerushalmi Megillah 1:5). It is not our purpose to inquire into the nature of this aggadah, but this much comes out explicitly: they thought that what is said, "and it was written in the book," means that they attached the words of Esther to the Writings. And it is also very likely that this is the plain sense of the verse. It appears that in their view the Holy Writings in the days of Mordecai and Esther were divided into Torah, Prophets and Writings, and the whole of the Writings was called "the book." This does not contradict our estimate placing the sealing in the last generations of the Men of the Great Assembly. For it is a clear matter that the Scroll of Esther that we have was composed at a time later than the event, as is seen clearly from several verses in this scroll (26–32); and in the time of the last writer the Holy Writings had already been sealed, and therefore it was hard in the eyes of the sages to attach the scroll to the Writings (see *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11), whose sealing had already taken place earlier. Now the basis of this aggadah stands firm: after the Holy Writings were sealed, they attached to them also the Scroll of Esther, whose time of composition, in the second letter,⚠1 is very late. And this agrees in part with another reasonable hypothesis that deserves to be mentioned here:{v1_05_18:2} namely, that the Holy Writings were not collected at one time. The first collection was very old; it included the Torah and the book of Joshua and was founded in the days of the First Temple. For this reason no more than the five books of the Torah and the book of Joshua are found among the Samaritans — although their book of Joshua has changed much from ours. The second collection was made after their return from the exile, and it includes also the Prophets; its seal is the last verses of the book of Malachi, from "Remember the Torah of Moses My servant" [Malachi 3:22] to the end of the book.{v1_05_19:1} The third collection was later; then the section of the Writings was added, namely most of the book of Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Ruth, the Song of Songs, Lamentations and Ecclesiastes, and the seal of the whole is the last verses of the book of Ecclesiastes. This was still under the rule of the Persians. And there was yet a fourth collection, which added the books of Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles, and its seal is the Scroll of Esther. This was in the time of the Maccabees. The book of Esther in the text before us was composed in the days of the Maccabees on the basis of manuscripts that they had from an early time. This book was needed in that time, when the wicked kingdom sought to destroy the Jews, as in the early time, in the days of Ahasuerus and the wicked Haman.

1.he: אשר זמן חבורה באגרת שנית מאוחר מאד
1.note: Elliptic; "the second letter" refers to Esther 9:29 ("this second letter of Purim"). Read: its composition, including the second letter, is very late.

rows.en: After all these things, there is one thing that we can hold with clarity: that the sealing of the Holy Writings and their division took place, at the latest, at the end of the days of the Great Assembly. This follows for us from clear hints in Scripture and from compelling proofs that lie in the events of the times, as we have seen before. Besides these, it appears that in every generation from the time of the Maccabees onward this opinion was taking root among the Jews. Already in the days of the Maccabees it was widespread among the people that the collection of the Holy Writings had been completed in an early time. A hint of this is found in the second book of Maccabees (2:13, 14). And as for the books of Maccabees, although we do not know the time of their composition exactly, it is at any rate clear that they were written while the rule of the Maccabees still stood on its base (*Urschrift* by Dr. A. Geiger, p. 206). The sages of the time of the destruction of the Temple speak of the division by which the Holy Writings were divided into three parts, Torah, Prophets, Writings, as of a matter well known and familiar from days of old (Megillah 7a); and it is self-evident that these parts were sealed and delimited from an early time. So too the saying "All the Holy Writings may be rescued from a fire" (Shabbat ch. 15, mishnah 1)⚠1 shows that there was a delimitation of the Holy Writings from long before. And that mishnah is very old, for early sages already disputed its meaning and the meaning of its companions. A great hint of the sealing of the Holy Writings is found in an aggadah that speaks about the prophecies that were fixed to be kept for the generations. It tells: many prophets arose for Israel, double the number of those who went out of Egypt, but a prophecy that was needed for the generations was written down, and one that was not needed for the generations was not written down (Megillah 14a). The inner idea of this aggadah is that they selected among the words of the prophets which prophecy was fit to be kept for the generations and which was not. And what is the chief idea of the sealing if not the selection of which of the writings or the prophecies should be brought into the body of the Holy Writings and which not? It is further told in a baraita about the writing of the individual Holy Writings: Moses wrote his book and the section of Balaam and Job; Joshua wrote his book and eight verses in the Torah; Samuel wrote his book and Judges and Ruth; David wrote the book of Psalms through ten elders; Jeremiah wrote his book and the book of Kings and Lamentations; Hezekiah and his company wrote Isaiah, Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes; the Men of the Great Assembly wrote Ezekiel and the Twelve, Daniel and the Scroll of Esther; Ezra wrote his book and the genealogy of Chronicles up to himself, and Nehemiah completed it (Bava Batra 15a). Now it is not our purpose to decide whether the details of these matters are founded on a true tradition or only on conjecture; but this much comes out explicitly, that their view was that there were several collectors at different times. And so we saw in the aggadah mentioned first, that each collector selected what was fit to be kept for the needs of the coming generations, and set aside and removed what was not needed. And since we have also seen that they thought that the Men of the Great Assembly were the last writers, it is self-evident that to them they attributed the last selection among the writings and the prophecies, which of them should be kept and which not; and this selection is itself the sealing of the Holy Writings. Josephus ben Gorion the priest⚠2 also speaks of an ancient division by which the Holy Writings were divided into three parts, and all of them together are twenty-two books, all of which are justly regarded as divine; and several writings that were written from the days of Artaxerxes until his own time were not regarded as so trustworthy as the ancient books, because prophecy had ceased (*Against Apion* 1:8). Now he does not state here his own opinion in particular, but tells us what the opinion was that had spread among the people. And we are informed also in the Talmud that this belief lived among the people. They believed that all the Holy Writings — whose number Josephus puts at twenty-two, and the sages of the Mishnah and the Talmud at twenty-four — were all given by the holy spirit, and that in them a Jew should toil to learn and to teach, and not in other books apart from these (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin ch. 10). The later sages exaggerated this matter in their figurative speech and said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said, I have written twenty-four books for you; take heed not to add to them (Numbers Rabbah ch. 14); for whoever brings into his house more than twenty-four books brings confusion into his house (Ecclesiastes Rabbah, at its end). And from an ancient tradition we have heard that at first they would say that Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes were hidden away, because they said these were parables and not of the Writings, and they went and hid them away, until the Men of the Great Assembly came and interpreted them (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 1).{v1_05_20:1} Now, besides the proofs that come from the sealing of the books of Ecclesiastes and of the Scroll of Esther, by which the antiquity of the sealing of the Holy Writings has been made clear, and besides all the hints given in several ancient aggadot, we have seen that the sages who lived in the time of the destruction of the Temple and before it spoke of the collection of the Holy Writings and of their division into three parts as of a matter well known and familiar from long before. And now, if we join to this the causes that compel the sealing of the Holy Writings in the last generation of the Men of the Great Assembly, it is neither wondrous nor far-fetched that we set the time of the sealing in this generation.

1.note: Printed so; the mishnah "All the Holy Writings may be rescued from a fire" is Shabbat 16:1.

2.note: Weiss's name for Josephus (Flavius Josephus); the reference is to Against Apion.

rows.en: From this time, when the Holy Writings were sealed, a special name arose for the other books that were not included among the Holy Writings, and they were called by the name "external books." Most of them, children of that time, are lost. The book of Ben Sira is one of the external books; of it we have small Hebrew remnants in the Talmud, and the whole of it is in a Greek translation. This book too is not included in the Holy Writings, although all of it is moral instruction in parable and figure, like the Proverbs of Solomon. The reason, without doubt, is that at the time this book was composed the Holy Writings had already been sealed; and not as the one who says (Hitzig, in his commentary on Psalms, 118) that no Hebrew copy was spread among the people, because the original book remained in the hand of his grandson, who took it with him when he went down to Egypt, and so the last collectors could not attach it to the Holy Writings. For how is it possible that the original book was lost, when after several hundred years we find it in the hands of the sages of the Talmud, who copied sayings from it? And when we see that the author asks the children of his people at the end of his book to meditate in it to learn wisdom and instruction, surely he made copies of his book in order to attain his wish and his aim. But on the other hand, we cannot bring a proof that the Holy Writings had necessarily been sealed before this, on the ground that otherwise they would have attached the book of Ben Sira to the Holy Writings; for even if he completed his book before the sealing, it is possible that it was not attached to the Holy Writings for another reason, namely because the author put his name on his book, and this was enough for those who sealed not to bring his book in among the Holy Writings. Yet the truth is indeed that the book of Ben Sira is later than the sealing, as we have seen from other proofs. However, even if after the sealing they did not add to the collection of the Holy Writings, nevertheless they did not refrain from time to time from breaking this statute in part, by adding individual sections to the ancient writings; for in this they did not see a breach of the statute, since the warning was only against making many books without end. All the psalms that were composed in the days of the Maccabees were not put together in a book of their own but were attached to the ancient book of Psalms, because they were strict about the warning against making separate books and adding to the Holy Writings, but they were not strict about adding sections to the books. Only for a great need did they turn aside from this and add a separate book, such as the Scroll of Esther, which they attached to the Holy Writings in the days of the Maccabees, as said above. And yet, on the contrary, we have seen that at a later time the fixed sealing did not hold them back from questioning it. For in the last half-century before the destruction of the Temple the sages gathered in the house of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon and wished to hide away the book of Ezekiel, and but for the efforts of Ḥananiah they would have hidden it away (Shabbat 13b; Ḥagigah 13a). It is also told that they sought to hide away the book of Ecclesiastes (Shabbat 30b), and the same is said of the book of Proverbs and the Song of Songs (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 1). And although this account moves the time of the event back to the days of the Men of the Great Assembly, the matter is not certain, and it seems more likely that all these hidings took place at one time, as will be made clear further below (ch. 22).

From the extreme warning by which they were warned not to make books there came also the restraint from writing words of Torah in general, so that they refrained from writing their teachings and their midrashim in a book. Now in this we find the first root of the prohibition of writing for all matters, new or old, that were received; for whatever was beyond these they took care not to write. But what the later authorities thought in this matter, that it was so intended by the Torah and hinted at in what is said, "Write thou these words" [Exodus 34:27] — these you write, but you do not write halakhot (Temurah 14b) — is a midrashic figure of speech. For from of old the prophets wrote their prophecies in a book, and several matters that are of the kind of laws are within their prophecies; and if we say that the statute from former times was that oral matters you are not permitted to say in writing, why did they write their traditions? True, one can answer this that the spirit of the Lord upon them gave them understanding; yet for this reason there is still no proof of the necessity that the matters be written, for we do not find that they were commanded or permitted to write the matters in a book. And according to the opinion of the sages of the Talmud, several prophets did not write their prophecies at all, and those who came after them wrote them (Bava Batra 14b); and who permitted them this? Therefore it can only be that from the time they were warned against making books without end, from then also they refrained from writing both halakhot and interpretations of the Torah, and not before. However, the cause of the restraint from writing their halakhot and their interpretations in a book lies in the nature of the interpretations and the halakhot. We have already seen above that the interpretations of the Torah depended on the agreement of the great court of each time (above, ch. 9), and the received traditions too were destined to expand; therefore it was more fitting for them to be expounded orally than to be written in a book (*Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, ch. 13), for when they are written in a book they are nailed fast and become a fixed statute, which is not so when they are expounded orally. Now this cause is indeed reasonable for the restraint from writing words of Torah and their interpretations and composing them into a book; but this cause does not hold with regard to writing such matters for the benefit of remembering them or for another purpose. Therefore we have no compelling cause to think that they refrained from writing anything small or great for their own use. And indeed a slight examination of the Talmudic literature from the first times shows the opposite. If we consider how much the old mishnayot, which are marked especially by their brevity and their language, differ from the mishnayot of the later generations, then we must necessarily decide that they are written remnants that the early ones wrote for themselves; especially since it was a rule and a duty with them that every man should say words of Torah in the language of his teacher. Therefore the disciples surely wrote for themselves the words of their teachers in order to know them in their exact language; for the mind cannot bear that so great a sum as the old halakhot remained in the memory of every single disciple in the exact language of the early ones, unless we say that they were recorded in writing with them. We further find that at times they turned aside from the habit and in time of need wrote down established matters⚠1 in a special scroll, as in the days of Ḥananiah ben Hezekiah ben Garon they wrote Megillat Ta'anit (Shabbat 13b). We also find that several sages departed from the habit. For in the days of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder a book of a Targum of Job was found, and this was without doubt by an early translator (Shabbat 115a); and every Targum was regarded by them as oral matter. And surely the Targum of Job was not the first that they wrote down; rather, Targums of other books too were with them in writing at that time (Zunz, *Gottesdienstliche Vorträge*, p. 62). So too the Greek translation of the Seventy was in writing, and whoever studies that translation will find in it several oral interpretations; and there was no one among the sages who questioned it on the ground that it is not permitted to write; rather it is said that the day on which this translation was given was hard for Israel because the Torah cannot be translated adequately (Tractate Soferim ch. 1). Not only that, but from this story — if it is indeed an old tradition — we can bring a clear proof that the masters of the Talmud too thought that the early ones did not refrain from writing words of tradition. For although their saying that the day was hard for Israel because the Torah cannot be translated adequately may mean the same as what the grandson of Ben Sira said about his Greek translation, in which he translated the book of his grandfather (in the preface to his translation), that the Greek version of the Holy Writings is not able to attain the force of the Hebrew language in every way, nevertheless it is also possible, and more in agreement with the views of the sages of the Talmud, to say that the reason the Torah cannot be translated adequately is that the translators, according to the aim they had before them, had to translate the words according to their plain sense, while the Torah must be interpreted according to its midrash. And so we see that even in the view of the sages, had the translators been able to interpret and translate adequately, it would not have occurred to them to question this matter on the ground of the prohibition of writing.

1.note: Printed so; the phrase is odd. Read as "established (fixed) matters", i.e. decisions that stood.

rows.en: But at a later time this prohibition reached a new level. When other sects arose in the midst of our people, which turned far from the faith of their fathers' tradition, countless various scrolls were written according to the new opinions, also in the Hebrew, Aramaic or Syriac language. We have a small remnant of one of these scrolls in the Aramaic language (Shabbat 115b). At that time the habit became a fixed statute. R. Ishmael, who lived at the end of the first century of the rise of this sect, is the one from whom the first hint of the prohibition of writing halakhot has reached us. His disciples brought in his name in these words: "Write thou these words" [Exodus 34:27] — these you write, but you do not write halakhot (Temurah 14b). And whoever considers the multitude of the midrashim of the Gnostics and of other scrolls full of midrashim, which were written at the end of the aforementioned first century and also after it, will find that they were compelled to make a fence about the matter and to warn against writing new books in general. The aforementioned cause through which they upheld the prohibition of writing is hinted at in an aggadah which a Talmudic sage put figuratively in the form of a conversation between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Moses: When the Holy One, blessed be He, said "Write thou," Moses asked that the Mishnah too be in writing; but because the Holy One, blessed be He, foresaw that the nations of the world would in future translate the Torah and read it in Greek, and they would say, "We are Israel," and until now the scales are evenly balanced, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: You say that you are My children; I know only that those who hold My mysteries are [My children]; and which is that? The Mishnah (Tanḥuma, Ki Tissa). The core of this aggadah is told in different forms (Exodus Rabbah ch. 47; Numbers Rabbah ch. 14), and from this we see that the basis of the aggadah and its idea had already been forgotten by them. But its basis is to show that the cause of the restraint from writing oral matters lies in the rise of the aforementioned faith, when writings in the form of midrashim spread, and they were compelled to warn against writing. And we already know that such extreme warnings are mostly proofs of a habit to the contrary. Therefore, from the fact that they were so strict in warning, we see that the custom was to write. But it is hard for us to prove that this warning had a lasting effect on all the sages of that time and after it, so that we should say that from that time onward all of them refrained from writing anything of halakhah and midrash, even a single letter (Rashi, Eruvin 62b); for there are trustworthy proofs that in every time sages departed from the custom and wrote books and scrolls. True, an excuse is offered for these scrolls, and they are called by the name "hidden scrolls," which they would write and put away in hiding (Shabbat 6b, and Rashi's commentary). But what does the hiding help, if from of old the prohibition of writing stood as a fixed statute? Moreover, besides the scrolls that were called hidden scrolls, we find that there were scrolls written by the greatest of the sages, such as the Ribbit of the school of R. Ḥiyya (Bava Metzia 62b), the Nezikin of the school of Karna (Sanhedrin 30b), and the Kiddushin of the school of Levi; and one of the later sages found an ancient Tosefta (Yerushalmi Shabbat 8:1); and Levi had written mishnayot and corrected them (Yevamot 10a); and R. Jeremiah said to R. Zerika, "Go, look in your Mekhilta" (Gittin 44a); and R. Yoḥanan, who heard of the existence of the baraitot arranged in the Sifra, went and learned them in three days and reasoned over them three months (Yevamot 72b), and it is not said from whom he learned them, so surely the Sifra existed in writing. And all the more so in aggadic midrash, in which there were many written books, among them the Aggadeta of the school of Rav (Sanhedrin 57a), and books of aggadah that were before R. Joshua ben Levi (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:2) and that were before R. Yoḥanan (Gittin 60a); and R. Abba, the brother of R. Ḥiyya, would write aggadot in a book (Yerushalmi Shabbat, ibid.). Here we have before us that despite all the warnings by which they were warned, they wrote down every kind of words of Torah. In this account we have gone several steps ahead on the path of time, in our wish to show that in all times the sages did not keep this warning with great strictness and were not strict about it, but wrote oral matters in a book. In short, it is clear that the beginning of the warning against writing books on matters of Torah was because they did not want to make the Oral Torah, which is destined to expand, fixed and cut off. Later they fenced this in even more because of the spread of the sect of the minim. But nevertheless the sages did not refrain, for themselves, from writing for the purpose of memory; and all that many of the sages after the Talmud, down to the latest generations, have decided in order to prove the opposite of this is built only on fine points of detail, which, if we pass over them with a spirit of faithful criticism, are gone and are no more.{v1_05_23:1}

footnotes.en: In the introductory books to the Holy Writings there is great confusion regarding their sealing. Some put their sealing as late as the time of the Maccabees, when the public reading of the books of the Prophets began, and therefore they were compelled to bring the Holy Writings into one collection (Hävernick, in the name of Clericus, vol. 1, p. 68). For this view a proof was brought from the fact that in the book of Daniel there are matters that cannot be earlier than the time of the Maccabees (Bauer, in his Introduction, p. 36). Others say that a collection was made in the days of Nehemiah, and they relied on what is written in the second book of Maccabees, 2:13–14, where the collection of the books made by Nehemiah is explicitly mentioned (Bleek, in Hävernick, 69); and a second collection was made in the time of the Maccabees. And who can count all the imagined hypotheses with which the aforementioned scholars and their many companions who wrote on this question have contented themselves?⚠1 But in my opinion the clearest proof is from the seal of the book of Ecclesiastes, as I wrote in the text; and what is nearer to reason is what follows for us from the aggadah of the Talmud, that the sealing was early, and therefore it was hard for the sages to attach the scroll to the Holy Writings. But even though they did not add to the books, nevertheless they added sections to individual books, as we have made clear.⚠2 And see the book *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11, which dwells on this at length with several reasonable arguments; and see also the book *Gottesdienstliche Vorträge* by R. Yom Tov Zunz, p. 34.
